title: On-Prem Trust Argumentation Framework for Audit Committees - Draft
content:
Objective:
- Equip AE/SE and GTM stakeholders with a concise, audit-friendly argument map to present Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane) to audit committees, internal compliance officers, and procurement for regulated workloads.

Scope and audience:
- Primary: Audit committees, internal auditors, CISO office, compliance leads.
- Secondary: CTO/VP Engineering, procurement, legal.

One-line executive claim:
- "Redwood Private provides an auditable, customer-controlled inference environment that preserves developer ergonomics while enabling compliance teams to retain custody and oversight of sensitive data and controls."

Decision anchors auditors care about (how we map answers):
1) Data custody and residency: who touches plaintext? where is metadata stored? retention windows?
2) Access control & segregation: how is admin access scoped and audited? multi-tenant isolation?
3) Cryptographic controls: KMS/HSM integration, key lifecycle, where keys are stored and who can rotate them?
4) Observability and audit artifacts: what logs exist, retention, tamper-evidence, exportability for SOC audits?
5) Patch/upgrade & vulnerability management: how are runtime images patched, what SLAs exist for CVE response?
6) Third-party dependencies and supply chain: OSS components, SBOM availability, signed artifacts.
7) Data flows & threat model: where are tokens/caches persisted (disk, memory), network egress patterns, fallback behaviors.

Control-plane language to use (short phrases auditors understand):
- Customer-managed control plane: "Control plane components (auth, routing, telemetry) are deployed into the customer's VPC and governed by their network controls and IAM."
- No-plaintext-exfil policy: "Transit and persistent stores can be configured to never persist unencrypted model inputs/outputs outside the customer's secured environment."
- KMS-backed key custody: "Customer KMS/HSM is the root for encryption and signing; Redwood has no access to unwrapped keys."
- Audit-first telemetry: "All admin actions and inference routing decisions produce immutable audit logs that can be shipped to customer SIEM/Syslog."
- Deterministic downgrade/fallback: "When a model fallback occurs, policy files enumerate whether payloads are routed to lower tiers and how data is handled during fallback."

Suggested short narratives by persona:
- For Audit/Internal Risk: "Redwood Private puts the control plane inside your trust boundary. We integrate with your KMS, ship logs to your SIEM, and produce a signed SBOM. That makes evidence collection for audits straightforward and under your control."
- For CISO: "We minimize attack surface by running model serving and control services in your VPC; keys never leave your KMS, and admin actions are subject to your IAM and MFA policies."
- For Procurement: "Deployments can be air-gapped or VPC-isolated, with optional on-prem runtime packaging and documented SLAs for patching and support."

Common buyer objections + short scripts (tone: technical, audit-friendly):
1) Objection: "How can we prove Redwood can't access our data?"
   Reply: "We provide a signed deployment manifest and KMS integration proof-of-responsibility: keys are customer-owned and unwrapped only within your environment. We also support renderable audit logs showing that control-plane operations were executed by your principals."
2) Objection: "What happens during upgrades — could data be exposed?"
   Reply: "Upgrades follow a documented build-and-sign pipeline. We provide SBOMs, signed images, and you can require local image verification. Runtime data paths remain subject to your KMS policies during upgrades."
3) Objection: "We're regulated — do you support evidence for SOC/FedRAMP?"
   Reply: "We supply artifact bundles for auditors: configuration manifests, logs, access lists, SBOMs, and a mapping of our controls to common frameworks. For sensitive buyers we offer a dedicated onboarding checklist to capture audit artifacts."
4) Objection: "Is latency impacted by having a customer control plane?"
   Reply: "Control plane locality only affects management and routing; inference can still execute on dedicated hardware in-region. We provide deployment patterns that colocate telemetry and routing components to minimize latency."

Competitor positioning notes (short):
- Big public cloud managed endpoints: strong on compliance posture via platform certs, weaker on inference economics and model-agnostic routing. Pitch: Redwood gives equivalent audit artifacts while allowing optimized inference runtimes and transparent cost controls.
- Inference-only SaaS vendors: may offer simple private installs but often ship telemetry/control to vendor backplane. Pitch: focus on custody — keys, logs, and manifests remain under customer control with Redwood Private.
- Self-built pipelines: expensive to maintain and audit. Pitch: Redwood provides off-the-shelf manifest + SBOM + logging artifacts to accelerate audits and reduce engineering burden.

Technical checklist to include in audit package (deliverables):
- Deployment manifest (YAML) with component versions and signatures
- Signed SBOM and image signatures
- KMS integration proof (key IDs, rotation policy, access policy snippet)
- Audit log export (sample) and schema description
- Network flow summary (egress endpoints, IP ranges, ports)
- Patch cadence and CVE response playbook summary
- Data retention & purge policy sample

Redwood differentiation bullets (concise):
- Unified API across hosted/dedicated/private so app code doesn't change when moving into a regulated environment.
- Cryptographic custody: customer KMS/HSM-first model with no vendor-unwrapped keys.
- Audit-ready artifacts: signed manifests, SBOM, logs, and mapping to standard frameworks.
- Operational controls: deterministic fallbacks, policy-first routing, and per-route cost/latency SLOs.

Sample slide titles for an audit committee deck (6 slides):
1) "Control Plane in Your Trust Boundary: What that means"
2) "Data Flow & Custody: Keys, Logs, and Evidence"
3) "Patch & SBOM Hygiene: How we reduce supply-chain risk"
4) "Audit Artifacts: What you'll get for SOC/FedRAMP/ISO"
5) "Operational Scenarios: Fallbacks, Outages, and Forensics"
6) "Next steps: Evaluation checklist and sandbox timeline"

Action items / next steps (ownership):
- Create audit artifact template bundle (owner: Ravi Menon) — due 2025-11-20
- Produce a short demo script showing KMS handshake and log export (owner: Lina Torres) — due 2025-11-10
- Draft 6-slide audit-committee deck with speaker notes (owner: Evelyn Park) — due 2025-11-06

Open questions (for engineering/product):
- Can we provide a non-prod signed image verification flow that customers can run locally before installing?
- What is the minimal SBOM we can reliably produce for every release?

Notes to seller/SE (talking tips):
- Always lead with custody: auditors respond to tangible ownership (keys, logs, manifests).
- Avoid promising certifications; instead show artifacts and a repeatable evidence-gathering process.
- Use concrete examples: "We shipped X audit bundle for a healthcare pilot last quarter; here's how long it took." (If permitted, replace with anonymized case studies.)

Appendix: quick glossary for audit committees
- Control plane: services that manage routing, auth, telemetry — can be vendor-managed or customer-managed.
- SBOM: Software Bill of Materials, list of components in an image.
- KMS/HSM: Key Management Service / Hardware Security Module — where encryption keys are stored and managed.
- Manifest: signed description of deployed components and versions.

End of draft.
